chapters.1: After Joshua's death, the tribes of Judah and Simeon lead the ongoing conquest of Canaan, capturing cities like Jerusalem and Hebron and punishing the cruel king Adonibezek as he had punished others. The chapter also lists several tribes, including Benjamin, Manasseh, and Dan, that fail to fully drive out the Canaanites from their territories, leaving them to live alongside Israel.
chapters.2: An angel rebukes Israel for failing to destroy the Canaanites' altars and for making alliances with them despite God's command. After Joshua's generation dies, a new generation arises that doesn't know the Lord, falls into idolatry, and the chapter explains the repeating cycle of the book: Israel sins, God allows oppression, Israel cries out, and God raises up a judge to deliver them.
chapters.3: This chapter introduces several judges: Othniel defeats the king of Mesopotamia and gives Israel peace for a time; Ehud, by a clever ruse, assassinates the oppressive Moabite king Eglon and leads Israel to defeat Moab; and Shamgar strikes down six hundred Philistines.
chapters.4: Israel falls under the oppression of Canaanite king Jabin and his military commander Sisera, who has nine hundred iron chariots. The prophetess Deborah commissions Barak to lead Israel's forces, and after Israel defeats Sisera's army, Sisera himself is killed by a woman named Jael, who drives a tent peg through his temple while he sleeps.
chapters.5: This chapter is the victory song of Deborah and Barak celebrating Israel's defeat of Sisera, praising God's power and the tribes who joined the fight while criticizing those who stayed home. It also honors Jael for killing Sisera and vividly describes Sisera's anxious mother waiting for a son who will never return.
chapters.6: Midianite raiders oppress Israel severely, destroying their crops, until God calls Gideon, a reluctant farmer, to deliver his people. Gideon asks for signs to confirm the call, including the famous test with dew and a fleece, and he tears down his family's altar to Baal, provoking local anger.
chapters.7: God has Gideon reduce his army from thousands down to just three hundred men through a water-drinking test, to make clear that victory comes from God, not numbers. Using trumpets, torches, and a nighttime surprise attack, Gideon's small force throws the vast Midianite camp into confused panic and rout.
chapters.8: Gideon pursues and captures the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, punishing the Israelite towns of Succoth and Penuel for refusing to help him during the chase. Though offered kingship, Gideon declines, but he makes a gold ephod that later becomes an object of idolatrous worship, and the chapter ends noting his death and Israel's quick return to Baal worship.
chapters.9: Gideon's son Abimelech murders nearly all his seventy half-brothers to seize power over Shechem, sparing only Jotham, who denounces him with a parable about trees choosing a worthless bramble as king. Abimelech's violent rule eventually collapses as Shechem revolts against him and he is killed during a siege when a woman drops a millstone on his head.
chapters.10: The judges Tola and Jair lead Israel for a combined span of about 45 years with little detail given. Israel again turns to idolatry and is oppressed by the Ammonites and Philistines, and when the people cry out, God initially responds that they have forsaken him too many times, though he is ultimately moved by their distress.
chapters.11: Jephthah, a skilled fighter rejected by his family because his mother was not his father's wife, is recalled by Gilead's elders to lead them against the invading Ammonites. Before battle he makes a rash vow to sacrifice whatever comes out of his house to greet him if he wins, and tragically this turns out to be his own daughter, whom he must fulfill the vow regarding.
chapters.12: A conflict erupts between Jephthah's forces and the tribe of Ephraim, who are angry at being excluded from the fight against Ammon; the dispute escalates into a civil war where Gileadites identify fleeing Ephraimites by their mispronunciation of the word "Shibboleth." The chapter then briefly lists three minor judges — Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon — who follow Jephthah.
chapters.13: An angel appears to a barren woman, the wife of Manoah, announcing she will bear a son who is to be raised as a Nazirite dedicated to God and who will begin delivering Israel from the Philistines. The couple offers a sacrifice during which the angel miraculously ascends in the flame, and the promised son, Samson, is born and grows under God's blessing.
chapters.14: Samson insists on marrying a Philistine woman from Timnah against his parents' wishes, and along the way he kills a lion with his bare hands, later using a riddle based on honey found in its carcass at his wedding feast. When his Philistine guests cheat to solve the riddle, Samson's anger leads to violence, and his bride is given to another man.
chapters.15: In retaliation for losing his wife, Samson burns the Philistines' crops using foxes with torches tied to their tails, prompting a cycle of revenge that leads the Philistines to kill his former wife and father-in-law. Samson slaughters many Philistines in response, and after being handed over by his own people, he breaks free from his bonds and kills a thousand more using only a donkey's jawbone.
chapters.16: Samson becomes entangled with Delilah, who repeatedly tries to learn the secret of his strength on behalf of the Philistines, and he toys with false answers until he finally reveals that his power is tied to his uncut Nazirite hair. Betrayed and shaved while asleep, Samson is captured, blinded, and enslaved, but in a final act he pulls down the pillars of a Philistine temple, killing himself along with many enemies.
chapters.17: A man named Micah sets up a private shrine with an idol made from silver his mother had dedicated, and hires a wandering Levite to serve as his personal priest. The chapter notes the troubling state of Israel at the time, when "every man did that which was right in his own eyes," with no king to enforce proper worship.
chapters.18: The tribe of Dan, still lacking enough land, sends scouts who discover and later seize Micah's idols and priest on their way to conquer the peaceful city of Laish. They rename the captured city Dan and set up Micah's idol there, establishing an illegitimate center of worship that persists for generations.
chapters.19: A Levite's concubine is brutally abused and killed by men of the town of Gibeah in the territory of Benjamin after the townspeople threaten the Levite himself. In horror and outrage, the Levite cuts her body into pieces and sends them to all the tribes of Israel as a shocking call to justice.
chapters.20: Outraged by the crime at Gibeah, the tribes of Israel unite to demand that Benjamin hand over the guilty men, but Benjamin refuses and defends them, leading to a brutal civil war. After early setbacks, Israel's forces ultimately crush Benjamin's army, nearly wiping out the entire tribe.
chapters.21: Realizing they have sworn not to give their daughters in marriage to the nearly annihilated tribe of Benjamin, the other Israelites look for a way to provide the surviving Benjamite men with wives without breaking their oath. They do this first by attacking Jabesh-gilead for not joining the war and taking its young women, and then by allowing the Benjamites to seize wives from dancers at a festival in Shiloh, closing the book on a chaotic, lawless period.
